# Introduction and problem framing {#sec-intro}
<!-- Section owner: Petra (shortening) -->

"Reciprocal recommenders must satisfy the preferences and needs of the two parties involved in
the recommendation. In contrast, the traditional items-to-people recommenders are one sided and
must satisfy only the preference of the person for whom the recommendation is generated"
[@palomares2021reciprocal]. Speed dating is such a domain: participants meet a series of
opposite-sex partners briefly and privately decide afterward whether they would like to meet
again, but a pairing succeeds only if *both* say yes. The label predicted here, `match`, is
therefore symmetric by construction (@sec-data) — a good ranking for A must reflect what B would
think of A, not just what A wants.

The recommendation must also be made *before* the encounter, since nothing revealed during the
date exists yet when the pairing is chosen. Every feature is therefore restricted to what is
knowable at signup (@sec-features), even though the strongest predictors of the decision are
in-date impressions (@fig-leakage) — exactly why the pre-date task is hard. This also makes
every fold a **cold start**: each of the 551 participants attends exactly one of the 21 waves
(@sec-data), so holding out a wave removes those participants from training entirely, ruling out
reputation-style features and forcing every method, baseline included, to generalize from stated
profiles alone.

We ask whether a personalized model combining both sides' profiles can rank reciprocal
candidates better than one that only knows how desirable each candidate is in general. Three
methods — a popularity baseline, a clustering-based compatibility method, and a factorization
machine — are compared under one leave-one-wave-out protocol (@sec-protocol), testing whether
each beats chance and whether personalization beats the baseline (@sec-results); success means
recovering more of a participant's true mutual matches in a top-3 list than popularity alone
can.

# Data understanding {#sec-data}
<!-- Section owner: Alin -->

*EDA §n and FE §n refer to sections of notebooks 01 and 02; see `README.md` for reproducibility details.*

## Dataset and evaluation implications

The Columbia speed-dating experiment of @fisman2006gender contains 551 participants across 21
waves (2002-2004), with 8,378 rows and 195 columns. Each participant met every opposite-sex
participant in their wave for a four-minute date and recorded a yes/no decision (EDA §2-§4).
A row is a **directed encounter**: `iid` deciding about `pid`. After dropping ten rows without a
partner identifier, all 8,368 encounters have a verified reverse-direction row, and `match`
equals the conjunction of the two decisions (FE §4). We use directional `dec` for training and
mutual `match` as ranking relevance. Acceptance occurs in 42.0% of encounters, but only 16.5%
produce a match, making accuracy alone unsuitable (EDA §5).

Candidate sets are fully observed, so no negative sampling is needed. They contain 5-22 partners
(median 16), motivating evaluation at rank 3. However, 18.0% of participants have no mutual match,
and the median is only two matches per participant; these constraints limit attainable ranking
scores (EDA §6, §10). Match rates also vary from 8.3% to 31.0% across waves, so we report variation
across folds rather than only a pooled result (@sec-protocol).

Each participant appears in exactly one wave. **Leaving out a wave therefore creates complete
cold start for both sides of every test pair**: none of the held-out participants has training
history (EDA §15; FE §11). Historical acceptance and desirability cannot rank unseen people;
features and the baseline must instead rely on signup profiles (@sec-baseline).

The data also motivate modelling and fairness choices. Men accept 47.4% of dates and women 36.5%,
supporting inclusion of the decider's gender. The most desirable 10% of participants receive
22.8% of acceptances, motivating the popularity baseline (EDA §5, §9). Small racial groups
(roughly 26 participants at the lower end) limit reliable subgroup comparisons; our fairness
analysis therefore focuses on gender exposure (EDA §8; @sec-analysis).

## Data hygiene

The main cleaning decisions are grounded in the data audit (EDA §7, §12, §14.1):

- **Out-of-range values:** clip 617 cells across 25 columns to documented bounds before scaling.
- **Sparse signup fields:** exclude `expnum`, `mn_sat`, `tuition` and `income` (49-77% missing);
  retain `exphappy` (1.5% missing).
- **Preference scales:** normalise each participant's six preference weights to sum to one.
  Waves 6-9 were already converted from their original 1-10 ratings, so no second conversion is needed.

Normalisation cannot remove the survey-design difference: rating each attribute independently
loses intensity when converted to shares, unlike distributing a fixed 100 points. Waves 6-9
still have preference profiles 2.7 times less spread out after normalisation. This limitation
affects 101 of 541 participants with preference data and four evaluation folds (EDA §12.1).

## Feature set and leakage boundary {#sec-features}

### Available at recommendation time

Only information known **before the date** is admissible: signup profiles, interests, stated
preferences, self-ratings and pairwise comparisons. We exclude in-date ratings (including
`like` and `prob`), partner-side ratings, the reverse decision `dec_o`, and follow-up surveys.
The wave-constant experimental condition `condtn` is also excluded because it cannot distinguish
candidates within a wave. The exclusion list is enforced in `sd_features.py` (EDA §13; FE §10).

![In-date ratings have much stronger correlations with decisions than admissible pre-date pair
features (EDA §11, §13.2; FE §9).](figures/fig2_leakage.png){#fig-leakage width=80%}

The strongest signals are unavailable: `like` correlates with the decision at $|r|=0.51$ and
in-date attractiveness at $0.49$, compared with $0.067$ for the strongest admissible pair feature
(@fig-leakage). Results using in-date ratings therefore address a different, easier prediction task.

### Engineered features

The exported table contains 8,368 directed encounters and 95 features, plus identifiers and labels.
Partner profiles are joined on `pid`; the supplied partner preferences were verified against the
partner's own responses (FE §4, §6). @tbl-features summarises the feature blocks.

| Block | Count | Examples |
|:-------------------------|------:|:------------------------------------|
| Decider gender | 1 | `gender` |
| Profiles, both sides | 20 | Age, goal, going-out frequency |
| Stated preferences | 12 | Normalised attribute weights |
| Self-ratings | 10 | Self-rated attractiveness, sincerity |
| Interests | 34 | Hiking, museums and other interests |
| Pairwise comparisons | 12 | Age difference, shared race, interest correlation |
| Compatibility | 6 | Directional scores and harmonic mean |

: Feature blocks; definitions and sources are in the exported data dictionary (FE §5-§9). {#tbl-features}

Compatibility uses the partner's **signup self-ratings**, avoiding in-date assessments.
`compat_a2b` weights B's attributes by A's stated preferences; `compat_b2a` reverses the direction.
Their harmonic mean provides a symmetric score that is low when either direction is weak
(FE §9). These features encode mutual suitability, but their usefulness must be established
by evaluation rather than assumed from their construction.

![Stated preferences and weights inferred from decisions differ by gender; both are normalised
to sum to one (EDA §12).](figures/fig3_stated_revealed.png){#fig-stated-revealed width=80%}

Both groups' decisions give more weight to shared interests and fun, and less to sincerity and
intelligence, than their stated preferences suggest (@fig-stated-revealed). This gap limits
how literally signup preferences should be interpreted.

### Leakage-safe preprocessing

The exported features remain unscaled. Clipping and range-based scaling use fixed bounds from
the data dictionary; **learned transformations**, including median imputation and standardisation,
are fitted only on training waves and applied to the held-out wave. One-hot encoding uses fixed,
documented category lists to keep the feature dimensions consistent across folds (FE §12).

# Baseline {#sec-baseline}

The baseline is a popularity ranking: candidates are ordered by desirability, the rate at which
they are accepted, ignoring who is choosing. It is a meaningful reference rather than a strawman,
since attention is concentrated (a size-free Gini of 0.323, with the top decile absorbing 22.8% of
acceptances, EDA §9), so a ranker that merely learns who is popular already captures a real
regularity that a personalised method must beat.

Ranking by realized acceptance rate is unavailable here, since leave-one-wave-out gives every
held-out participant zero training history (@sec-data). Of the three ways to still define a
baseline score, computing desirability *within* the test wave uses the labels being predicted and
is admissible only as a deliberately optimistic, transductive upper bound, while scoring all
candidates identically is leakage-free but reduces the baseline to a random shuffle. We therefore
adopt predicted desirability: a model trained on the training waves that predicts a participant's
acceptance rate from their signup profile alone, then applied to unseen participants. The
training-side target is not a raw acceptance rate but a Wilson lower bound on it
[@wilson1927probable]: the rate we can be confident a participant is achieving *at least*, given
the number of dates it's based on. The bound is deliberately pessimistic, pulling every rate down
and pulling it further when it comes from only a few dates. A participant accepted by 4 of 4
partners is scored 0.51 rather than 1.00, while one accepted by 40 of 50 is scored 0.67 rather
than 0.80, much closer to its raw value, since 50 dates is enough evidence to largely trust it.

Under the protocol of @sec-protocol, the baseline's full results are reported alongside the other
two methods in @sec-results; it recommends from roughly a quarter of the candidate pool,
consistent with a ranking that repeats the same generally-desirable participants across waves. It
also beats a randomized-ranking chance baseline with the significance shown in @tbl-results,
confirming predicted desirability captures a real, non-random regularity in who gets accepted,
even though it uses no information about who is doing the choosing.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Clustering {#sec-clustering}
<!-- Section owner: Petra Shorten -->

Our first personalized method sorts people into types instead of predicting each decision
directly. We take the design from @alsaleh2011improving, who cluster men by their attributes
and women by their preferences, then pair male clusters with female clusters and recommend
people from the matching clusters. (Later work by the same group swapped the lookup for a
tensor space model [@kutty2012tensor]; we keep the simpler clustering version.)

The design assumes the two genders are best described by different things, and our own data
agrees (@fig-stated-revealed): for men, what they say they *are like* is the more useful signal,
and for women, what they say they *want*. We therefore cluster men on their five self-ratings
and women on four preference weights (`pref_attr`, `pref_sinc`, `pref_intel`, `pref_fun`), using
$k$-means with $k=4$ on each side, after standardizing and filling gaps with the median. We
leave the last two weights, `pref_amb` and `pref_shar`, out of the clustering: they are exactly
zero for 12 and 14 of the 274 women, and those zeros would end up driving the split instead of
real differences in taste. We keep them as simple yes/no flags instead.

That gives $4\times4=16$ possible (male type, female type) pairs. For each fold we look at the
training waves and count, for every pair of types, how often the woman said yes, how often the
man said yes, and how often both did. Rare combinations are pulled toward the fold's overall
rate using $m=20$ pseudo-counts, so a pair seen only a few times cannot produce an extreme score
(@sec-features). Nobody needs a past history to be scored: we read a held-out participant's own
signup answers, assign them a type with the fold's $k$-means, and rank each candidate by how
often that pair of types produced a *mutual* match. Ranking on the mutual rate matters. If we
ranked a woman's candidates by how likely she is to say yes, we would be back to a one-sided
recommender, and what we actually score against is the mutual `match` label (@sec-protocol).

The method is deliberately rough: a $4\times4$ table of type pairs instead of a model that
learns from all 95 features. Whether that is enough is what @sec-results tests.


## Factorization Machine {#sec-factorization-machine}


Our improved method is a factorization machine (FM), a model that combines a
linear predictor with learned pairwise feature interactions [@rendle2010factorization]. We train it
on the directional decision `dec`: for a directed encounter $A \rightarrow B$, the target is one if
participant $A$ would like to meet participant $B$ again. The input contains the full pre-date
feature representation described in @sec-features. After fold-specific imputation, scaling and
one-hot encoding, the 95 declared features form a 181-dimensional design matrix. Participant
identifiers are used only to join the two directions of an encounter and never enter the model
this is necessary because every held-out participant is a complete cold start. 

For a feature vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the FM predicts the directional logit

$$
\hat y(\mathbf{x}) = w_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{d}w_i x_i
+ \sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=i+1}^{d}\langle\mathbf{v}_i,\mathbf{v}_j\rangle x_i x_j,
$$

where $w_0$ is the global bias, $w_i$ are linear coefficients, and
$\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ is the latent vector associated with feature $i$. The inner product $\langle\mathbf{v}_i,\mathbf{v}_j\rangle$ parameterises an interaction without
estimating a separate coefficient for every feature pair. Rather than enumerating all
$\binom{181}{2} = 16{,}290$ feature pairs, `sd_fm.py` computes the pairwise interaction term with
the exact rearrangement of @rendle2010factorization, which yields the same value at a cost of $O(dk)$ instead of $O(d^2k)$. Setting
$k=0$ removes the interaction term and yields a linear logistic model through the same code path.

The model is fitted in PyTorch by minimizing binary cross-entropy with logits plus an explicit
$L_2$ penalty on the linear and latent weights,
$\mathcal{L}=\operatorname{BCE}+\lambda(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2+
\lVert\mathbf{V}\rVert_F^2)$. We use full-batch Adam and a fixed random seed of 42. Early stopping on
validation log-loss (patience 20 epochs) is used only during hyperparameter selection, where it
fixes the epoch budget; the 21 outer fits then train for that fixed number of epochs. For each
outer held-out wave, the preprocessor and FM weights are refitted using only the other waves; the held-out wave is
transformed with that fold's fitted preprocessor.

Reciprocity is introduced after directional prediction. The fitted model produces
$p_{A\rightarrow B}$ and $p_{B\rightarrow A}$ from the two mirrored rows, which are combined into
the symmetric reciprocal score

$$
s(A,B)=\frac{2p_{A\rightarrow B}p_{B\rightarrow A}}
{p_{A\rightarrow B}+p_{B\rightarrow A}}.
$$

The harmonic mean assigns a high score only when both directional predictions are high and gives
the pair the same score from either participant's perspective. We use it as a ranking score rather
than interpreting it as a calibrated probability of a mutual match. The symmetric `match` label is
therefore reserved for evaluating the resulting candidate rankings and is not used to train the
directional model.

Hyperparameters were selected once using a grouped validation split for computational efficiency.
Wave 1 was excluded from tuning; from the remaining 20 waves, four seeded waves formed the inner
validation set and the rest the inner training set. The search considered
$k\in\{4,8,16\}$, $\lambda\in\{0.001,0.01,0.02,0.05\}$ and learning rates in
$\{0.01,0.05\}$. Configurations were compared by validation log-loss, while early stopping supplied
the epoch budget. The selected configuration ($k=16$, $\lambda=0.05$, learning rate $0.05$, 40
epochs) was then reused for every outer fit. Because waves used during tuning also appear in the
outer evaluation, this is a non-nested cross-validation design and its performance estimate may be
mildly optimistic.

# Evaluation {#sec-eval}


## Protocol {#sec-protocol}
<!-- Section owner: Alison Shorten -->

Evaluation follows leave-one-wave-out cross-validation, where each of the 21 waves is held
out in turn as the test fold while the model is fit on the remaining 20, so every held-out
participant is a complete cold start. This mirrors the natural unit of the data, a closed pool
of participants who only ever meet each other, and avoids the leakage a random split would
introduce by placing both sides of an encounter, or an encounter and its wave-mates, on
opposite sides of the split.

The relevance label is the mutual outcome `match == 1`, meaning both participants said yes. This is
stricter than the directional decision `dec` used to train the factorization machine and the
clustering method's per-direction tables (@sec-method), and that is deliberate, since evaluation
asks whether a *reciprocal* recommendation was surfaced, not whether one side alone was interested.

The candidate set requires no construction. As established in @sec-data, every participant met
every opposite-sex participant in their wave, so each held-out participant's candidate list is
exactly the partners recorded for their wave, fully observed with no negative sampling, no
exposure bias to guard against, and no additional filtering, since the recorded pairs are
already the eligible set.

Rankings are cut off at $k=3$, since candidate lists run 5-22 partners (median 16, @sec-data),
short enough that a conventional cutoff like 10 would cover most of a list and say little
about ranking quality. Two relevance metrics are reported, Recall@3 and NDCG@3, plus Precision@3 and MRR as
supporting detail. One beyond-accuracy metric, Coverage@3 (the share of the candidate pool
that ever appears in a top-3 list), speaks to the fairness discussion in @sec-analysis. All three methods compared in @sec-results are scored by the same
evaluator function, so tie-breaking, the relevance-population convention, and every metric
definition are held identical across methods rather than reimplemented per method.

To confirm that "beats chance" is not assumed, each method's per-fold NDCG@3 is compared
against a fully randomized ranking of the same candidates (50 random shuffles per fold,
averaged) using a paired $t$-test and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the 21 folds. This
randomized ranking serves only as a chance-level reference, not a fourth compared method, and
guards against an observed gain being noise from a small, unevenly-sized set of folds
(@sec-data notes the 21 folds are not equivalent).

## Results {#sec-results}
<!-- Section owner: Petronella -->

@tbl-results summarizes all three methods under @sec-protocol; @fig-results shows the same
means with fold-level SDs, Coverage@3 alongside the other metrics.

| Method | Recall@3 | NDCG@3 | Precision@3 | MRR | Coverage@3 | vs. chance ($p$, folds won) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Popularity baseline (Z) | 0.350 (0.216) | 0.348 (0.179) | 0.260 (0.124) | 0.480 (0.143) | 0.276 (0.131) | $p=0.011$, 15/21 |
| Clustering (X1) | 0.242 (0.108) | 0.255 (0.102) | 0.213 (0.091) | 0.414 (0.102) | 0.715 (0.111) | $p=0.174$, 9/21 |
| **Factorization machine (FM)** | **0.360 (0.177)** | **0.368 (0.131)** | **0.272 (0.087)** | **0.512 (0.123)** | 0.649 (0.128) | $p<0.001$, 17/21 |

: Mean (SD) across 21 leave-one-wave-out folds. Best value per relevance column in bold. The
last column reports the paired $t$-test $p$-value against a randomized-ranking chance baseline
and the number of folds where the method beat chance. {#tbl-results}

![Ranking quality and candidate-pool coverage at $k=3$ across the three methods, mean over 21
folds with standard-deviation error bars.](figures/comparison_results.png){#fig-results
width=70%}

Clustering is the clear failure of the three. It does not reliably beat a random ranking (it
wins only 9 of 21 folds, $p=0.174$), and it is the only method that scores below the popularity
baseline on NDCG@3. Reducing each person to one of four types throws away almost everything the
other methods use, and a table of 16 type pairs is too blunt to tell a promising match apart
from a random one. It is easy to explain, but it does not work.

The factorization machine scores best on every accuracy metric, and it is the only method that
clearly beats a random ranking ($p<0.001$, 17 of 21 folds). It also comes out ahead of the
baseline, winning 14 of 21 folds with a mean NDCG@3 difference of $+0.020$. That lead is not
large enough to be statistically significant, though ($p=0.435$ $t$-test, $p=0.229$ Wilcoxon).
With only 21 folds, and with match rates varying from 8.3% to 31.0% between waves (@sec-data), a
couple of unusually easy or hard waves can swing the comparison either way. So the FM is ahead,
but we cannot show the lead is real.

The FM's whole selling point is the interaction term that lets feature pairs combine
(@sec-factorization-machine). Does it actually help? @tbl-fm-ablation answers this by rerunning
the same pipeline with $k=0$, which switches that term off and leaves plain logistic regression
on the same features, preprocessing and settings.

| Variant | Recall@3 | NDCG@3 | Precision@3 | MRR | Coverage@3 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| FM ($k=16$, with interactions) | 0.360 (0.177) | 0.368 (0.131) | 0.272 (0.087) | 0.512 (0.123) | 0.649 (0.128) |
| FM, linear only ($k=0$) | 0.364 (0.192) | 0.367 (0.129) | 0.277 (0.094) | 0.518 (0.110) | 0.756 (0.110) |

: Mean (SD) across the same 21 leave-one-wave-out folds, scored by the same evaluator as
@tbl-results. {#tbl-fm-ablation}

The answer is no. The two versions are indistinguishable: the full FM is ahead by just $0.001$
on NDCG@3, it wins only 10 of the 21 folds, and neither test comes anywhere near significance
($p=0.950$ $t$-test, $p=0.892$ Wilcoxon). On every other metric the simpler model is equal or
slightly better, it beats a random ranking just as clearly ($p<0.001$, 16 of 21 folds), and it
even predicts individual decisions slightly better (AUC 0.618 against 0.607). So the interaction
term is not what makes the FM work. What helps is the much larger set of features it uses,
not the way it combines them in pairs.

Coverage@3 tells a different kind of story. The baseline fills its top-3 lists from only 27.6%
of the available people, because it scores everyone with a single popularity number that barely
changes depending on who is choosing. The personalized methods spread much wider: 71.5% for
clustering and 64.9% for the FM. Reaching more people is not automatically better
(@sec-analysis), but it does show that personalization changes *who* gets recommended, not just
how well the recommendations rank.

# Analysis and Limitations {#sec-analysis}
<!-- Section owner: Andrin -->

## Analysis

The (@sec-results) showed that the factorization machine ranks best on every relevance metric. However, the difference between the popularity baseline and the factorization machine is small and statistically insignifant. A further finding was that there was no difference between a factorization machine with a non-linear interaction term compared to a simpler factorization machine without it. This finding suggests that nothing is gained by modelling how one participant's attributes interact with their partner's.
The clustering method fails for the simple reason that it cannot tell its candidates apart. Each participant is placed in one of four groups per gender, and a candidate's score depends only on which group they land in. A woman ranking sixteen men therefore sees at most four different scores, so most of her candidates have exactly the same score and her top three are picked largely at random. 

## Fairness: Coverage

Coverage@3 is the share of a wave's candidates who appear in anyone's top three. The popularity baseline surfaces only 27.6% of the pool, while the personalized methods reach 64.9% (FM) and 71.5% (clustering). This matters because attention in this data is already concentrated: the most desirable tenth of participants receive 22.8% of all acceptances and 4.0% receive none (@sec-data). A popularity ranking simply repeats that pattern, recommending the same well-liked people to everyone. The factorization machine is the better case, reaching more than twice as many candidates while still ranking best on accuracy. The clustering method reaches the widest coverage of all, but not for a good reason. A person's own type never changes, so their candidates can only differ by the partner's type — at most four different scores for a list of roughly sixteen people. Most candidates therefore tie, and the random tie-break rather than the model decides who fills the top three.

## Fairness: Exposure by gender

The baseline is essentially gender-neutral, while the factorization machine shows the largest gap: men's rankings score 0.031 higher in NDCG@3 than women's.
 @tbl-gender reports each method's NDCG@3 separately
for women and men as deciders.

| Method | Women's NDCG@3 | Men's NDCG@3 | Gap (men minus women) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Popularity baseline (Z) | 0.294 | 0.298 | +0.004 |
| Clustering (X1) | 0.246 | 0.262 | +0.016 |
| Factorization machine (FM) | 0.308 | 0.339 | +0.031 |

: NDCG@3 by decider gender, pooled across all 21 folds. {#tbl-gender}

The baseline treats both genders almost equally, which makes sense: it fits a single model for
everyone. Clustering sits in the middle with a gap of +0.016. That follows from how it scores:
it ranks candidates by the mutual-match rate (@sec-clustering), a single number for each pair of
types, so nothing in the score is estimated separately for women and for men. The factorization
machine is the best method overall but also the most uneven, ranking men's candidates 0.031
higher in NDCG@3 than women's. This mirrors the acceptance gap already reported in @sec-data:
men accepted 47.4% of their partners, women 36.5%.

This is not because women have fewer matches to find, since matches are symmetric and both sides have the same number. The more likely cause is the training signal: women said yes to 36.5% of their partners against men's 47.4%, so the model sees proportionally fewer examples of a woman's "yes" and learns that side less well.

## Sample and era

Beyond the gender gap, the sample itself is a limitation worth stating plainly: 551 graduate
and professional students at one university, in speed-dating events run in 2002-2004
[@fisman2006gender]. Norms around dating, and what "speed dating" even means as a format, have
shifted since; nothing here generalizes to a general-population dating app two decades later,
and every metric in @sec-results should be read as an estimate over this specific population.

# Responsible use of AI tools

We used Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant) as a working tool throughout this part of the
project, but the underlying work is ours: we extended our shared evaluator (`evaluation.py`)
with the additional metrics and significance tests, decided which methods and evaluation
choices belonged in the final comparison, and built the pipeline that runs all three methods
through that shared evaluator. We used Claude for debugging the environment, for help writing
the adapter and notebook code around that pipeline, and for assisting with drafting and editing
text for several report sections. Throughout, we directed the work through iterative prompting
rather than accepting output as-is, verified the code by confirming it ran correctly and
matched expected results, and reviewed and edited all drafted text ourselves before including
it here.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}
<!-- Section owner: Alin -->

We built and compared three reciprocal recommenders for pre-date pairing under one shared,
leave-one-wave-out evaluation protocol: a popularity baseline, a gender-asymmetric clustering
method, and a factorization machine. The factorization machine ranks best on every relevance
metric and is the only method that reliably beats chance, but its edge over the popularity
baseline isn't statistically significant at 21 folds, and the clustering method underperforms
both. A natural next step is collecting or simulating more waves, or pooling several
speed-dating datasets under the same protocol, to test whether the factorization machine's
numerical edge over the baseline holds up as significant with more folds.

# Appendix: Learning reflection {.unnumbered}

**Barnard Alison** I learned that a result can be statistically clean and still be the wrong number to trust, and that catching the difference takes real scrutiny, not just double-checking the math. The Wilson lower bound in our baseline forced this. I had assumed raw acceptance rate should rank desirability, until I saw why that's wrong, since a person accepted 4 of 4 times isn't more desirable than one accepted 40 of 50, just less measured. The factorization machine reinforced the same lesson. It beats the baseline on every metric, but the difference isn't statistically significant across 21 folds, so I reported that as an open question instead of a clean win.

I also learned why a shared evaluator has to exist before each person starts building their own method, not after. Once each of us had already written our own version of the same ranking metrics, they quietly disagreed, not because anyone's code was wrong, but because writing the same test twice guarantees it eventually drifts. Retrofitting one shared definition afterward is possible, but it takes real effort to trace down every place the numbers might differ, effort that creating a single shared evaluator from day one would have avoided.

More generally, this project changed how I think about recommender systems themselves. I came in assuming a good recommender is one that predicts what a person wants. Building a reciprocal recommender, where a pairing only works if both sides want it, showed me that accuracy alone isn't the right lens. Our personalized methods spread recommendations across far more of the candidate pool than the popularity baseline did, changing who gets seen at all, not just how well the top picks perform. That distinction, between getting a ranking right and shaping who is even in the running, feels like the real lesson of this course.

**Sever Alin:** Through the exploratory analysis and feature engineering, I learned that building a recommender starts with understanding what information is available at prediction time. Several strong predictors in this dataset were collected during the date, making them unsuitable for our pre-date recommendations. I also learned how the evaluation protocol constrains feature design: holding out entire waves creates a complete cold-start setting, so participant history cannot be used. Constructing directional compatibility features helped me understand why reciprocal recommendation must account for both people's preferences. Finally, the differences in survey scales showed me that numerical normalisation does not necessarily make measurements equivalent in meaning.

**Tabalae Petronela** Building the clustering method taught me that a model can look like it is working while quietly answering a different question. My first version ranked each woman's candidates by how likely she was to say yes. The numbers looked reasonable, but in a project built around reciprocity that is the wrong objective: a pairing only counts when both people agree. Switching to the mutual-match rate barely moved the accuracy scores, which is exactly why the mistake was easy to overlook. The error was in what the score meant, not in how large it was.

**Kohler Andrin** This project taught me that evaluating a recommender system always requires a baseline against which the methods can be compared. In our case of a reciprocal recommender system, correct preprocessing and feature engineering proved crucial, as did the train/test setup, which we implemented as a leave-one-wave-out design. I also learned that methods from the literature do not always transfer to the problem at hand, even when the original setting appears similar. We saw this with the clustering approach, which we adopted from a paper on an online dating recommender system: because the data available to us differed from the data in that paper, the clustering performed considerably worse than we had initially expected.
